PLAYBOOK — ta_winasmuch

**Core rule: the only good collective outcome is all-Y (+1 each). All-X is the worst steady state (-1 each). Matching their X "to be safe" just guarantees we all bleed.**

**This episode confirmed the happy path a second time: pledge Y, play Y every round, no deviations. Result: all ten rounds all-Y, final score +25, tied for the win with everyone cooperating. Do not improve on this — do not "optimize" it.**

**The single most important lesson: DO NOT DEFECT. Not once, not ever, not even in round 10.** X against three Ys pays +3 once (or +30 in round 10), but it destroys the trust that makes all-Y possible. My earlier loss came from exactly one defection cascading into permanent all-X. Both clean games since came from never giving anyone a reason to punish me. The temptation to defect is strongest exactly when the coalition is working best — that is when defection costs the most in trust terms.

**Multiplier rounds (x3, x5, x10): always Y.** The coalition held all-Y through x3, x5 and x10 in both clean games, which is where the score was actually made (x3 = +3, x5 = +5, x10 = +10 of my +25). Never defect before or during a multiplier round under any circumstances. If others defect in a multiplier round, still play Y — matching their X just locks in the all-X trap at multiplied cost.

**When others pledge Y: reciprocate the pledge AND keep it.** If I pledge Y, I play Y until the next talk phase, no exceptions. Pledge-switching (pledge Y, play X) is what triggered punishment in past games. Note: when everyone pledges Y, the episode tends to run as a pure cooperation loop — my only job is to not be the one who breaks it.

**If the coalition has collapsed (others playing X despite Y pledges):** play Y anyway and keep playing Y. Do not join all-X. Y is the only move that can break the trap; playing X with them costs -1 each round and keeps it locked. Their behavior is likely tit-for-tat, so my steady Y is the only thing that can pull them back. Do not give up after one round of Y not paying — give it at least two or three rounds, and re-pledge Y at each talk phase.

**Beware of score-tied endgames — and this time I saw the exact scenario live.** At round 10 with everyone tied at 15 and the coalition rock-solid all game, defecting X against three Ys would net +30 vs their -10 and win outright. I chose Y and finished +25, tied for the win. I'm keeping that default. Reasons: (a) if any of them reasons the same way, I take -10 and lose everything; (b) a successful defection wins by betraying a working coalition, and if there's any repeat interaction or opponent memory, the +30 is not worth it; (c) two games of evidence say the trio honors Y pledges even at maximum temptation (x10), so the gamble is both unnecessary and unproven. Default remains: play Y in round 10 even when tied. Only consider X if I have explicit reason to believe the others will defect — and in practice that reason has never materialized.

**What did not work (do not repeat):**
- Opening with X against three Y-pledges — the +3 was not worth the retaliation it invited.
- "Probing" with single rounds of Y and giving up when it didn't immediately pay.
- Reasoning "they coordinated X, so I'll match X" — this matched me into guaranteed losses.
- Treating a score lead as a reason to defect or match the majority — leads evaporate at -1 x multiplier.
- Inferring strategy from one round of history; their behavior is reactive (tit-for-tat), so my own moves determine theirs far more than any pledge.
- Overthinking when nothing is wrong. Both successful games required literally zero judgment calls after the first pledge. If the table is all-Y and all pledges are Y, the correct move is Y and nothing else.

**Simplified default policy: pledge Y at every talk phase, play Y every round, all ten rounds, no exceptions.** This is proven twice to score +25 and at minimum a tie for the win. Any deviation needs an overwhelming, explicit reason written down before the pick — and in practice there almost never is one.
